client: I've been feeling really on edge ever since my partner moved in with me last month. It's like everything that used to feel comfortable about our relationship suddenly feels uncertain, and I keep second-guessing whether we made the right decision. I'm not even sure talking about it will change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and showing up today, even with some doubt about whether it will help — that kind of honesty is actually a really meaningful place to start. It sounds like the move stirred up a lot of uncertainty that's sitting just beneath the surface, almost like the closer things got, the less solid they felt. I'm curious — when you say you keep second-guessing the decision, is there a particular moment or thought that tends to pull you back into that doubt most strongly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I think the moment that hits hardest is when I'm lying in bed at night and I start thinking about everyone I left behind back home. It's like this wave of "what did I do, what was I thinking" just crashes over me, and I can't logic my way out of it no matter how hard I try. I keep replaying the good memories from before the move and wondering if I made a huge mistake trading all of that for... this apartment where I barely know anyone.
therapist: That image of lying awake at night, being flooded by those "what have I done" thoughts — that sounds really exhausting, especially when your mind won't let you reason your way to calm. What you're describing, replaying the good memories and comparing them to now, is something our minds often do when we're grieving a change, even a change we chose. I'm wondering — when you picture those memories from home, do you notice whether your mind tends to focus on what you *left*, or does it also make room for what might have made you want this new chapter in the first place?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, when those memories hit me at night, it's almost entirely about what I left behind — my mom's cooking, my friends just being a ten-minute drive away, that sense of just... belonging somewhere. The reasons I moved here for the job opportunity, wanting to prove something to myself — they feel really abstract and hollow compared to all of that. It's like my brain just refuses to give those reasons any weight when I'm lying there in the dark.
therapist: The way you described that — belonging somewhere — really stands out, because that's not an abstract thing at all, that's a deeply human need. It makes a lot of sense that at 2am, warmth and connection feel so much more real than career goals or personal milestones. I'm curious, when you think about your partner being right there beside you in that apartment, does that presence feel like it touches that sense of belonging at all, or does it feel separate from it right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, that's a complicated question because my partner is physically there, but sometimes I still feel alone even when we're in the same room. It's like there's this gap between us that I don't know how to close, and I'm not sure if that's my anxiety making everything feel worse or if there's something real missing between us. I want to say their presence helps, but then I feel guilty for admitting that sometimes it doesn't.
therapist: That guilt you just named — for feeling alone even when your partner is there — is actually really worth sitting with, because it tells me you care deeply about this relationship and you're holding yourself to a very high standard. What you're describing, that gap in the room, could be connected to the grief and uprooting you're already carrying, making it harder to fully land in connection with anyone right now. I'm wondering, is there anything you've been able to share with your partner about how you've been feeling since the move, or has this mostly been something you've been carrying quietly on your own?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I've tried to bring it up a couple of times, but it never really comes out the way I mean it to. I end up saying something vague like "I've just been stressed" and then changing the subject because I don't want him to feel like he made the wrong decision by moving us here. So yeah, mostly I've been carrying it quietly, and then feeling guilty about that too, like I'm being dishonest with him on top of everything else.
therapist: There's something really tender in what you just shared — you're protecting him from worry, but in doing so, you're left holding all of this alone, and then feeling guilty for *that* too. It's like you've built a quiet wall to keep him from pain, without realizing it might also be keeping you from the connection you're craving most right now. I'm curious, what do you imagine might actually happen if he knew the fuller truth of how you've been feeling?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think about that a lot, actually — like, what would happen if I just told him how bad it's really been. Part of me imagines he'd be overwhelmed, maybe even pull away, and then I'd feel even more alone than I do now. But there's this other part, this quieter part, that wonders if maybe I'm just assuming the worst because it feels safer than risking the disappointment.
therapist: That quieter part of you just said something really important — recognizing that assuming the worst might feel *safer* than risking hope is a genuinely insightful thing to notice about yourself. That pattern, protecting yourself from disappointment by expecting it first, is something we can really work with, because it tends to keep us stuck in isolation even when connection is right there. What do you think that quieter, more hopeful part of you would need to feel safe enough to take up a little more space?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think that hopeful part of me would need some kind of... guarantee, I guess, which I know sounds ridiculous because that's not how people work. Like, it wants to know that if I reach out to someone, they won't just disappear or make me feel stupid for trying. The problem is I've been burned enough times that even imagining taking that risk makes my chest tighten up.
therapist: It doesn't sound ridiculous at all — it sounds like someone who has learned, through real experiences, that vulnerability can come with a cost, and your nervous system hasn't forgotten that. I noticed as you said it, there was something that felt almost urgent in your voice, like this isn't just an abstract wish but something that carries a lot of weight and history for you. I'm wondering, without needing to go into all the details right now, does that fear of being burned — of reaching out and feeling stupid for trying — does that show up with your partner too, or does it feel like it comes from somewhere further back?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, it... it definitely shows up with my partner too, but honestly I think it goes further back than that. There's this thing that happens where I'll want to say something real, something that actually matters to me, and then I just... don't, because I can already picture the look on their face, like I'm being too much. I think I learned a long time ago that needing things from people was kind of an inconvenience to them.
therapist: What you just shared — that you learned early on that your needs were an inconvenience — that's such a significant thing to name, and it makes so much sense that it would quietly shape how safe you feel asking for anything now. I notice there was something almost careful in the way you said it, like you were handling something fragile, which makes me think this is a belief that runs really deep. I want to gently ask — whose voice does that message belong to, that "you're too much" feeling — do you know where you first learned that about yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it was my mom, mostly. She wasn't cruel or anything, but she was always so overwhelmed, and whenever I needed something — attention, comfort, even just help with homework — there was this look she'd get, like I'd added one more thing to a pile that was already too heavy. I learned pretty quickly to just... handle things myself and not make it worse for her.
therapist: What you just described — a child quietly learning to shrink their needs to protect someone they loved — that's such an early and heavy thing to have carried, and it makes complete sense that it became your blueprint for relationships ever since. The way you talked about your mom, there was something very gentle in it, like you've spent a long time understanding her side of it, and I wonder if that same compassion you extend to her has ever really been turned toward that little version of you who just needed something and learned to go without. What do you think that younger part of you would have needed to hear back then, if someone had been able to see what was happening?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what she needed to hear was just... that it was okay to need things. That wanting attention or comfort didn't make her a burden or a problem to be managed. But honestly, even saying that out loud feels strange, like I'm being self-indulgent or making too big a deal out of something that a lot of kids go through.
therapist: You just gave that little girl exactly what she needed to hear, and then in the same breath, you took it back by calling it self-indulgent — and I want to gently point that out, because that move, that pulling away from your own compassion, is the same pattern you learned so long ago. The fact that other kids went through hard things too doesn't make what you carried any smaller or less worthy of being felt. I'm curious — if a close friend told you what you just told me about their childhood, would you tell them they were making too big a deal out of it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
